query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate to an elevated temperature (around 500°C) during the additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys will reduce thermal gradients and residual stresses during processing, thereby decreasing fabrication‐induced defects (e.g., cracks and porosity) and improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of the final component.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited high-entropy alloy parts fabricated via laser-based AM (e.g., SLM or DED) at room-temperature substrate conditions that exhibit pronounced thermal gradients, resulting in cracking, porosity, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.intervention: Implement continuous substrate preheating (targeting ~500°C) throughout the AM build process.
generation.conditions: Laser-based additive manufacturing performed in an inert atmosphere using high-entropy alloy powders, where all other process parameters (laser power, scan speed, hatch distance, etc.) remain constant; the only variation is the substrate temperature being elevated by preheating.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction of steep thermal gradients leads to a more uniform cooling profile, which minimizes the development of residual stresses and promotes homogenized microstructure formation across layers.
generation.mechanism: Elevated substrate temperature slows down the cooling rate and reduces differential heat contraction. This mitigates the formation of high residual stress concentrations that normally induce cracking and porosity, ultimately yielding parts with improved dimensional stability and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to parts fabricated on a room-temperature substrate, components built with preheated substrates will show a lower density of cracks and porosity, reduced warpage and dimensional deviations, and enhanced mechanical properties such as higher tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Standard additive manufacturing using room-temperature substrates, where rapid cooling and steep thermal gradients are common, leading to significant residual stress and defect formation.
generation.boundary: The proposed benefit is expected to hold under typical laser-based AM conditions; however, the effectiveness may vary with specific alloy compositions, different AM technologies, or if preheating causes unintended side effects (e.g., oxidation or phase changes) at excessively high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports substrate preheating as a means to reduce cracking and defects, the optimal temperature and its quantitative effect on mechanical properties and dimensional precision may differ among various HEA systems and AM setups, requiring further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of high-entropy alloy samples under identical AM parameters except for substrate temperature. One set is built using the standard room-temperature substrate and the other using a preheated substrate at ~500°C. Compare the resulting parts for dimensional accuracy, defect density, and mechanical performance.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy and warpage (using coordinate measuring machines or 3D scanning)
Crack and porosity density (via SEM and/or micro-CT imaging)
Mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation (via standard mechanical testing)
Residual stress levels (using X-ray diffraction or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples produced with substrate preheating do not show a statistically significant reduction in defects, improved dimensional precision, and enhanced mechanical properties relative to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The conventional manufacturing of refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) for high-temperature applications is complicated, particularly when material costs and high melting points of the materials processed are considered. Additive manufacturing (AM) could provide an effective alternative. However, the extreme temperatures involved represent significant challenges for manufacturing defect-free alloys using this approach. To address this issue, we investigated the preparation of a CrNbTiZr quaternary complex concentrated alloy from an equimolar blend of elemental powders using commercially available powder-blown L-DED technology. Initially, the alloys exhibited some defects owing to the internal stress caused by the temperature gradients. This was subsequently resolved by optimizing the deposition strategy. SEM, XRD and EDS were used to analyze the alloy in the as-deposited condition, revealing a BCC phase and a secondary Laves phase. Furthermore, Vickers hardness testing demonstrated a correlation between the hardness and the volume fraction of the Laves phase. The present study demonstrates that a strategic combination of deposition-parameters optimization and thermal management enables the fabrication of a crack-free bulk CrNbTiZr RCCA via L-DED using elemental powders. This represents a significant advancement, as prior efforts involving DED of similar systems have typically been limited to thin-wall geometries and have often suffered from severe cracking, substantial residual porosity, or incomplete fusion [,,,,,,]. Our results indicate that insulating the build platform and minimizing the dwell time between the layers elevates the overall temperature of the sample, effectively preventing the formation of macrocracks. It can be attributed to the fact that the deposition on insulated substrate reduces temperature gradients created at the edge of the melt pool which in turn decreases the strain concentrations and suppresses the formation of cracks. In contrast, samples deposited on the thermally conductive platform exhibited pronounced cracking. A laser-induced pre-heating temperature of approximately 500 °C was determined to be adequate to achieve this effect.
